scenes.name: Hard rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El hard rock marca el fin de los creativos sesenta: sigue basado en el blues, pero más rápido, ruidoso y fuerte, y entierra el sufrimiento negro bajo miles de decibelios. Precedido por Cream, Blue Cheer y Guess Who, lo definen Led Zeppelin, hijos del blues que lo tocan como música para el cuerpo y que imponen el LP como formato del rock. En Gran Bretaña, Free, Status Quo, Thin Lizzy, UFO, Uriah Heep, Slade, Faces, Deep Purple (el estereotipo del género), Black Sabbath (cimientos del black y el doom metal) y Queen, los bromistas del movimiento. En EE UU, Mountain, James Gang, Grand Funk Railroad, Montrose, Bachman-Turner Overdrive y Heart.

podcast.title: One-Night-Only Reunion (2007)
podcast.body: Led Zeppelin reunited for a single, historic concert at the O2 in London on December 10, 2007. This event was prompted by the death of Ahmet Ertegun, the founder of Atlantic Records, who had signed the band in the late 1960s and was crucial to their rise. The lineup included Jimmy Page, Robert Plant, and John Paul Jones, with John's son, Jason Bonham, filling in on drums for his late father. It was the first significant appearance for Led Zeppelin in 27 years, attracting an overwhelming 20 million ticket applications. The band performed a 16-song set that night, but despite the massive success and acclaim, they have not played together again since. "On December 10th, 2007, Led Zeppelin reunited for a one night only concert at the O2 in London."

Jeff picked up the guitar at age 5, discovered Rush, Kiss, and various prog rock bands, and received his first electric guitar at age 12. "One of the people Tim left behind was his eight-year-old son, Jeff, who admitted his father only once. Mom was a classically trained musician playing piano and cello. xref.body: John Bonham, the drummer for Led Zeppelin, is mentioned as the father of Jason Bonham, who also became a drummer and filled in for him. "Jason Bonham is the son of Zepdrummer John."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Prodigy and Rebellion
xref.body: Tori Amos was the rebellious daughter of a minister and a musical prodigy. At the age of five, she earned a scholarship to the Peabody Institute at John Hopkins University in Baltimore. However, she was expelled at 11 for being "too rock and roll" for the classical curriculum, as her biggest influence was Led Zeppelin, not just classical composers like Debussy. "She was kicked out at the age of 11 for being a little too rock and roll for the curriculum. Dubuces was fine, but her biggest influence was Led Zeppelin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

xref.title: Not an Alternative Music Influence
xref.body: The Beatles are mentioned as an example of a band whose sound was explicitly *not* the lineage from which "alternative" music of the early 90s (like grunge) descended, distinguishing it from punk and new wave. "alternative was being used to describe a new generation of music that had descended from punk and new wave and not from Led Zeppelin and the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Operation Just Cause Playlist
xref.body: Motley Crue's music was part of the playlist used by the US Army during Operation Just Cause in December 1989. This music was blasted at the Vatican Embassy in Panama City to force Manuel Noriega out. "There was Motley Crew, there was Led Zeppelin, there was ACDC, it was actually quite the playlist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Perception as New vs. Old
xref.body: When Greta Van Fleet emerged in 2017, younger audiences perceived them as "new and fresh." However, older generations, particularly boomers and Gen Xers, immediately drew comparisons to Led Zeppelin's sound from 1971, illustrating a generational divide in musical perception and the phenomenon of musical styles being independently rediscovered. "The kids thought they were new and fresh. But God, didn't Led Zeppelin sound like this in 1971?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

xref.title: Peter Grant's Sexist Rejection of Heart
xref.body: Peter Grant, Led Zeppelin's manager and a co-founder of Swan Song Records, allegedly dismissed a cassette from Heart as "rubbish" after only a few seconds, solely because the band was female-fronted and featured a woman as the lead guitarist, illustrating prevalent sexism in the music industry. "Grant allegedly listened to a few seconds of this cassette and immediately classified it as rubbish. Why? Well, because they were not only female fronted, but also because the lead guitarist was a woman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Guitar Riffs
xref.body: Black Sabbath is credited with originating many great guitar riffs, which they claimed for all time due to being among the first to establish these powerful musical foundations. This pioneering work has had a lasting impact on rock and metal music. "Bands like Black Sabbath and Led Zeppelin got to so many of the great guitar riffs first and thus have claimed them for all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

xref.title: Pioneers of Heavy Metal (Mid-1970s)
xref.body: Black Sabbath is recognized as one of the seminal bands that emerged in the mid-1970s, whose "loud, heavy guitar rock" sound played a crucial role in shaping and popularizing the heavy metal genre. "But once heavy metal was introduced into the music vernacular, other people began to pick it up and use it to describe a new wave of loud, heavy guitar rock as groups like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Deep Purple began their rise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of Heavy Metal (Mid-1970s)
xref.body: Deep Purple is cited as one of the influential bands whose "loud, heavy guitar rock" sound contributed to the definition and popularization of the heavy metal genre starting in the mid-1970s. "But once heavy metal was introduced into the music vernacular, other people began to pick it up and use it to describe a new wave of loud, heavy guitar rock as groups like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Deep Purple began their rise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Preference for Loud Rock
xref.body: Black Sabbath is mentioned as one of the bands exemplifying the "big, loud rock" that Dave Grohl enjoyed in his youth, alongside Led Zeppelin, Kiss, and Rush. "But as much as Dave loved big, loud rock like Zepelin and KISS and Rosh and Black Sabbath, that would eventually take a left turn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer Role for Butthole Surfers
xref.body: John Paul Jones, widely recognized as the bass player for Led Zeppelin, also took on a producing role for the Butthole Surfers. He produced their 1993 track, "The Annoying Song," from the album "Independent Worms Saloon." "By the way, that song was produced by John Paul Jones, the bass player for Let's Set Plane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reggae Led Zeppelin Covers
xref.body: Dread Zeppelin's core concept was playing reggae covers of Led Zeppelin songs, a pursuit they took seriously despite initial perceptions as a novelty act. "They were pretty serious about what they were doing, which was playing reggae covers of Led Zeppelin songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roadie for Legendary Bands
xref.body: Henry "the Horse" Smith was a renowned roadie who worked for several iconic bands, including The Yardbirds, Led Zeppelin, and Aerosmith, showcasing his extensive experience in the music industry. "There's Henry the horse Smith, who humped gear for the yardbirds Led Zeppelin and Error Smith."

xref.title: Signing with Atlantic Records
xref.body: The band ultimately signed an 80/20 split deal with Atlantic Records for the world and America, while Warner Canada retained rights for Canada. This decision was influenced by the legendary status of Atlantic, known for artists like Led Zeppelin. They even met Ahmet Ertegun, one of Atlantic's co-founders, in his office on the day of signing, where they saw Jimmy Page's bow from "The Song Remains the Same" on the wall. "And so we decided to go with Atlantic records, which was the originally in our guys that we had seen that came up."

xref.title: St. Paul Origins and Early Influences
xref.body: Chad Smith, a hard-hitting and rock-solid drummer, started playing drums at the age of seven in St. Paul, Minnesota. Initially, he was a straight-ahead rock drummer, taking inspiration from bands like Black Sabbath, The Rolling Stones, The Beatles, The Who, and Led Zeppelin. "He's from St. Paul, Minnesota, started playing when he was seven."

xref.title: Stadium Rock Era
xref.body: By 1973, The Rolling Stones, alongside bands like Led Zeppelin and The Who, had "graduated" to playing stadiums, becoming multi-millionaires living in mansions. This perceived detachment from the everyday fan was one of the reasons a "reboot" for rock and roll was sought, leading to the rise of punk. "Second, rock had graduated to playing stadiums, Led Zeppelin, the Rolling Stones, the Who."

xref.title: Supergroup Formation
xref.body: Them Crooked Vultures was formed as a supergroup, bringing together Josh Homme, Foo Fighters' Dave Grohl, and Led Zeppelin's bass player John Paul Jones. "Josh was one-third of them crooked vultures, a supergroup that featured Buddy Dave Grohl and Led Zeppelin bass player John Paul Jones."

xref.title: Supergroup Formation (Years Ago)
xref.body: The band formed after years of casual discussions among Dave Grohl (Foo Fighters), Josh Homme (Queens of the Stone Age), and John Paul Jones (Led Zeppelin) about creating music together. They finally decided to make it a reality. "After years of joking about forming a band together, Dave Grohl of the Fung Fighters, Josh Hommie of Queens of the Stone Age, and Led Zeppelin's John Paul Jones decided to make it happen with them crooked vultures."

xref.title: Ticketron's Challenges with Major Shows
xref.body: By the late 1980s, Ticketron struggled significantly to handle the volume of requests for major shows like those by the Rolling Stones. Their computer systems were overwhelmed, leading to processing times of up to five minutes per request, which forced Ticketron to revert to selling physical, hard tickets for these high-demand events. "It got so bad that for big shows, Rolling Stone, Led Zeppelin II examples, the Ticketron had to become a seller of hard tickets just like the old days."

xref.title: Tragic Accidental Drowning
xref.body: On the evening of May 29, 1997, while in Memphis to record new material, Jeff Buckley went for a swim in Wolf River Harbor, which connects to the Mississippi River. He had swum there before, but this time he entered the water fully clothed and wearing heavy boots. While floating on his back and singing the chorus to Led Zeppelin's "Whole Lotta Love," a boat passed by, creating a wake that caused him to disappear. His body was found five days later downstream. The death was ruled an accidental drowning, with no drugs or alcohol involved and no indication of suicide. He was 30 years old. "Everything was going absolutely according to plan until the evening of May 29, 1997. Jeff was in Memphis to record some new material, and that night he and Keith Fulti, a rodean is banned, sat on the bank of Wolf River Harbor, which is connected to the Mississippi River, listening to music. Jeff had gone swimming there a few times before, and decided to do it again. So he went into the water. This time he was fully clothed and wearing big, heavy boots. He floated out on his back and began seeing the chorus to Led Zeppelin's whole lot of love. But then a boat came by, stirring up a big wake, and with that, Jeff was gone. His body was found five days later down River. No drugs, no alcohol, nothing to indicate suicide. It was a straight, accidental drowning. He was 30 years old."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Uncertain Future Post-Taylor Hawkins' Death
xref.body: The Foo Fighters face an uncertain future following the death of Taylor Hawkins, who was considered irreplaceable due to his chemistry and friendship with Dave Grohl and his essential role in the band's "family nature." Comparisons are drawn to Led Zeppelin, which disbanded after John Bonham's death, and Rush, which retired after Neil Peart's death. "What do the Fufighters do now? We don't know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Vocal Style Development
xref.body: Formed in 2012, Josh Kiszka, the singer, initially lacked his own vocal amplifiers. This forced him to develop a powerful vocal style to be heard over the guitars and drums, which, according to Jake Kiszka, naturally evolved into his Robert Plant-like delivery, likely also influenced by their exposure to old Led Zeppelin records. "Josh, for example, didn't have his own vocal amps, so he had to develop a style where he could be heard over the guitars and drums. And according to Jake, which is what he told me, this is how John ended up with that Robert Plant-like delivery."
